claim: The News Mill reports, on police sources, that around 15 Delhi Police personnel were injured, some women personnel reportedly by bites, and around 110 people were detained when the Indian Youth Congress marched from Raisina Road towards Jantar Mantar on a Sunday. The page carries no police statement on its own account.
notes: The police account of injuries to police is recorded because it is part of what happened and because an account that holds only protesters' allegations would be one-sided. One outlet, anonymous police sources, no statement on the record. The date is not settled by this source: the page was read as dating the protest to Sunday 5 October, and 5 October 2026 is a Monday; the Sunday of that weekend is 4 October. The archive has not corrected the source and records the date as the Sunday after 3 October.

claim: Delhi Police refused permission for the protest planned at Jantar Mantar on 2 October 2026. DT Next reports it on unnamed police sources and says the protest was called by AISA, a Rajya Sabha member and a Supreme Court lawyer. Deccan Chronicle reports police saying permission had not been granted and the AAP saying letters seeking it were sent about a week earlier. Bar and Bench reports a Delhi Police order dated 1 October 2026 rejecting the Indian Youth Congress application for permission to demonstrate there.
notes: The Indian Youth Congress order of 1 October is a written instrument with a date, and the Youth Congress has put it before the Delhi High Court (PROC-DEL-005), so a copy exists outside the police. It is the Delhi counterpart of the Maharashtra refusal at INC-MAH-003 and the Kochi notice at INC-KER-001. None of the sources names the officer or office that signed it. See OQ-061 and FQ-023.

sources.originates_from: Unnamed police sources

claim: IBTimes India reports that Delhi Police personnel at the Jantar Mantar protests did not wear name tags, that junior personnel were allowed to remove them while most IPS officers kept theirs, and that officials gave the reason as preventing individual officers being identified and targeted on social media after the protest of 20 July, with junior personnel assured that no action would follow if they acted within the law.
notes: One outlet. Hindustan Times and The Times of India headlines in the 5 October sweep carry the same story and were not retrieved. The record matters to this archive for a plain reason: an officer who cannot be identified cannot be asked who gave an order, and the explanation offered concerns harassment of officers and their families, which is a real harm and is recorded as the police's stated reason and not as the archive's view.

claim: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during the Jantar Mantar protest of 3 October 2026, that no FIR was registered when they went to a police station, and that Delhi Police transferred the complaints to the Crime Branch for what an unnamed New Delhi district officer called a fair and impartial enquiry. PTI reports that the Crime Branch said it would examine the allegations and record statements, and that the Press Club of India expressed concern and urged immediate action.
notes: The complainants are not named here. PTI reports that an Assistant Commissioner of Police is named in the complaint and could not be reached for comment; the officer is not named in this record, on the rule that an unproven allegation does not put a name in the archive. Deccan Chronicle reports that protesters and opposition figures say police cited the Crime Branch inquiry as the reason for deferring an FIR. Whether an FIR has since been registered is OQ-057. This is the same set of complaints The Week reports at INC-DEL-016, in different words.

sources.originates_from: PTI

claim: Bar and Bench reports that the president of the Indian Youth Congress moved the Delhi High Court on 3 October 2026 against Delhi Police's order of 1 October 2026 rejecting the organisation's application for permission to protest against the Chief Election Commissioner at Jantar Mantar. PTI, as carried by Deccan Chronicle, reports that on Friday 9 October 2026 a bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma declined an urgent hearing, with the Acting Chief Justice asking what the urgency was, and said the matter would be listed on Monday 12 October. The same report says the organisation had applied on 25 September for 100 to 150 people from 1 to 25 October, and that the petition asks the Court to quash the police communication of 1 October and direct fresh consideration of the request.
notes: Two outlets with different origins report the petition and the order of 1 October. The case number is not reported in either. No order on the merits exists yet. The hearing of 12 October is a date to check. Retrieving the petition and the order of 1 October is FQ-023.

sources.originates_from: PTI

claim: LiveLaw reports that on 5 October 2026 a bench headed by the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, agreed to list a plea seeking directions to Delhi Police to permit peaceful protests at Jantar Mantar, titled Priya Mishra v. Union of India, Diary No. 62121/2026. The Chief Justice is quoted as saying that if similar matters are pending the Court will find out, and that it will only list the matter.
notes: One source retrieved. Other outlets carry the story and were not read. Listing is not a hearing and no order on the merits is recorded. The petition and any order are to be retrieved from the Court's own site, as for FQ-016 and FQ-018.

claim: The Tribune reports that on Tuesday 6 October 2026 about 300 opposition MPs marched from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, that police stopped the march near NITI Aayog, and that several leaders were detained.
notes: One outlet, and the account of the first day is a summary inside a report about the second. The Wire carries a report headlined as Delhi Police detaining Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi during the INDIA bloc protest, but only its headline could be read, so it is not cited for anything here. The Election Commission is reported elsewhere to have said no party had sought an appointment before the march; that is not recorded here because the page carrying it was not read.

claim: On Wednesday 7 October 2026 Delhi Police detained opposition leaders near Jantar Mantar, among them Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. The Tribune and Siasat both report that Rahul Gandhi was taken to Barakhamba Road police station and released within hours, and report that Priyanka Gandhi was taken to Chhatrasal Stadium. The Tribune reports that police stopped three buses carrying MPs near the Janpath and Ashoka Road crossing for nearly two hours, and that other detained leaders included Deepender Singh Hooda and Derek O'Brien. Siasat reports that security personnel told protesters that section 163 was in force.
notes: Two outlets agree on who was detained, where they were taken and that they were released the same day. Neither quotes a police statement. Siasat's wording is 'BNS 163', which is the section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and not of the Nyaya Sanhita; the archive records it as section 163 and has not corrected the source. Whether an order was in force on 7 October, and whether it is the order of 2 October recorded at INC-DEL-012, is part of OQ-055.

sources.originates_from: PTI inputs, as stated in the article

claim: The Tribune reports that Priyanka Gandhi Vadra said police assaulted protesters and that she had been scratched and thrown to the ground, that Mahua Moitra alleged protesters were manhandled and accused police of using force, and that Jairam Ramesh said leaders were dragged away. The report carries no statement from Delhi Police.
notes: These are allegations by named politicians, reported as theirs. The Tribune also reports that women police personnel removed Priyanka Gandhi Vadra from the road where she was lying down, which is the police side of the same event and is not an allegation. No footage, medical record or police account is held.

claim: Siasat, with PTI inputs, refers to an FIR registered against Rahul Gandhi, which Akhilesh Yadav is reported to have tied to the protest of Tuesday 6 October 2026. The article gives no police station, no sections and no complainant, and quotes no police statement.
notes: The FIR is mentioned in a photo caption and in a politician's remark, and the article does not describe it. A search result summarised it as an FIR for entering Akashvani Bhawan without permission; the page read does not say that, and the archive does not record it. See OQ-062.

sources.originates_from: PTI inputs, as stated in the article

claim: FIR No. 110/2016 was registered at Police Station Vasant Kunj North, Delhi, over the event held at Jawaharlal Nehru University on 9 February 2016. The Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016 records it as registered under Sections 124-A and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and records the State's status report as saying the case was by then under investigation under Sections 124-A, 120-B, 34, 147 and 149.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: Both orders name the FIR number and station. The registration date is not stated in either order; the High Court order says in paragraph 27 that the FIR 'has been registered only about three weeks back'. LiveLaw (14 January 2019) gives 11 February 2016 as the registration date, a single secondary source (see HIST-JNU16-002). Sedition is the label the FIR carries; no finding on the merits is recorded here, and the High Court order itself says its observations are not an expression on merits.

claim: The FIR was registered on 11 February 2016 against unidentified persons following complaints from a Member of Parliament of the BJP (named in the report as Maheish Girri) and from the ABVP, under Sections 124A and 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
notes: Single secondary source, published 14 January 2019, describing the chargesheet. The complainant detail is not in the two court orders read for this file. A different account is recorded by the State in the High Court (HIST-JNU16-003): that the FIR followed a Zee News telecast of 10 February and raw footage obtained from the channel. Both accounts may be true. The archive has not seen the FIR itself. Obtain the FIR text (Delhi Police publishes FIRs online in many cases; check) to settle complainant and date.

claim: In the Delhi High Court on 2 March 2016 the Additional Solicitor General for the State submitted that: permission for a cultural evening at Sabarmati Dhaba, JNU, on 9 February 2016 had been granted on 8 February; JNU authorities cancelled it on learning of posters about Afzal Guru and Maqbool Bhatt; the Chief Security Officer of JNU and the local police were informed; local police and security staff positioned themselves between two groups of students; and, after a Zee News telecast on 10 February 2016, raw footage was obtained from the channel and FIR No. 110/2016 was registered. The order records this as the State's submission.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: VERIFIED only as to what the order records the State as having submitted. The order does not find these facts. It also records the petitioner's contrary account (that he raised no anti-national slogans, that the campus stayed peaceful, and that the video was reported to be doctored) in paragraphs 7 to 9, and the Standing Counsel for the Government of NCT of Delhi saying the petitioner could be released on bail (paragraph 25). This is the only primary document read that describes who informed the police before 12 February; it describes a call to police on 9 February, not an order to enter the campus on 12 February.

claim: Kanhaiya Kumar, president of the JNU Students' Union, was arrested by Delhi Police on 12 February 2016 in connection with the sedition case, and was in police custody until 17 February 2016 and in judicial custody until 2 March 2016.

sources.originates_from: Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: The Quint (16 February 2016) and The News Minute (25 February 2016) are independent outlets. The Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016 (paragraph 8) records the petitioner's submission that he had been remanded to police custody three times; it does not give the arrest date. Whether the arrest took place on campus, and in what manner, is covered at HIST-JNU16-005.

claim: Delhi Police went onto the JNU campus on 12 February 2016 and took Kanhaiya Kumar into custody there.

sources.originates_from: JNU status report to the HRD ministry, as reported

notes: The claim is widely repeated, but no source fetched for this file states the place, time and manner of the arrest in terms. The Quint (20 February 2016) says the Vice-Chancellor was criticised for not following protocol before police were allowed onto the campus, and gives no date. Onmanorama (15 February 2016) reports a JNU status report saying a letter was sent to police asking them to take utmost precautions before entering the campus, and that police told the university they would enter only if absolutely necessary. Search-result snippets, not read as pages, describe a plainclothes arrest from the campus and raids on hostels on 12 and 13 February; they are not relied on. Not found: a police arrest memo, the case diary entry, or a court record of the place of arrest.

claim: A letter from the JNU Registrar is reported by The Quint to have said that the Vice-Chancellor granted the police permission to enter the campus 'if need be and as you may deem fit'.
notes: Single secondary source read (The Quint, 20 February 2016, which calls it a 'virtual carte blanche'). The letter itself has not been seen; HuffPost India, citing NDTV, is reported in search snippets to describe it as 'purportedly' written by the Registrar, but that page could not be fetched (404 on the redirect) and is not cited as read. The Vice-Chancellor is reported in snippets to have said at a press conference that he did not invite the police; no fetched page carries that statement, so no DISPUTED record can be made yet. Obtain the letter by RTI to JNU and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, and the register entry for it. The Quint also reports a senior professor's claim that the Vice-Chancellor first refused and relented after the Security Officer and the Registrar stressed the gravity of the charges; that is one person's account and is not established. Quote check, 10 October 2026: The Quint page does not give the letter's date (earlier drafts said 11 February 2016) or name its addressee (earlier drafts said the Deputy Commissioner of Police, South District), so both were removed. Establish them from the letter itself.

claim: On 22 February 2016 Delhi Police were reported to be waiting outside the JNU campus for the Vice-Chancellor's permission before entering to arrest students who had returned to campus, and the teachers' association said the Vice-Chancellor had assured them the police would not enter.
notes: The Quint live blog and IANS (via ummid.com) are two reports of one situation on 22 February 2016, which is after the 12 February events. It shows police treating the university's consent as a step they sought, which is relevant context for the question of who authorised entry on 12 February, but it is a different day and not evidence about that day. The IANS report quotes the Delhi Police Commissioner, asked whether police would enter JNU, as saying he was confident his team was competent to deal with the matter and that the investigating officer would choose the best available option.

claim: Who gave the order for Delhi Police to enter the JNU campus on 12 February 2016, and who gave the order to arrest Kanhaiya Kumar, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: No order, requisition, case-diary entry, deployment record or affidavit naming the authorising office has been found. What the documents read do show: (a) the State's account in the High Court of events up to 10 February (HIST-JNU16-003); (b) a reported Registrar's letter of 11 February about university permission (HIST-JNU16-006), which would show the university's consent and does not show who in the police or the Ministry decided to go in; (c) in Parliament, members of the Lok Sabha on 24 February 2016 criticised the Home Minister's public statements and the Commissioner's, and the Minister of Human Resource Development spoke about the permission slip and the university's own enquiry, but the record read contains no statement by the Government on who authorised the entry or the arrest (HIST-JNU16-021). Delhi Police reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs; that structure is stated in this repository's own notes, not established from a source fetched for this file. Routes: RTI to the Ministry of Home Affairs and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, for the arrest memo, the case diary, any requisition to or from JNU, and communications between the two; a question in Parliament; the Delhi High Court record of W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016, including the State's status report.

claim: The Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.) granted Kanhaiya Kumar interim bail for six months on 2 March 2016 on a personal bond of Rs 10,000 and one surety, preferably a JNU faculty member, with an undertaking not to participate actively or passively in any activity which may be termed anti-national and a bar on leaving the country without the court's permission. The order records that the investigation had been transferred to the Special Cell.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016, Kanhaiya Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi), W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016
sources.originates_from: Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.); the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: The order records at paragraph 27 that 'the investigation has now been transferred to Special Cell'; it does not say which office ordered the transfer or when. The order also records the Government of NCT of Delhi's Standing Counsel supporting bail and the ASG for the State opposing it (paragraphs 18 to 25). Paragraph 56 states the observations are for deciding bail only and are not an expression on merits.

claim: On 15 February 2016, at Patiala House Courts Complex, New Delhi, people described in reports as lawyers or persons in lawyers' robes assaulted students, teachers of JNU and journalists, while the case against Kanhaiya Kumar was scheduled to be heard.

sources.originates_from: Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: Three outlets (The News Minute 25 February 2016; Legally India/IANS 23 July 2016; The News Minute/PTI 24 February 2016). The News Minute and Legally India draw on different wires. The Supreme Court order of 17 February 2016 itself records that 'certain unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place in the court premises' on 15 February (HIST-JNU16-011). Police later charged three lawyers and a Delhi BJP legislator (HIST-JNU16-016). Injury counts are not established (HIST-JNU16-012).

claim: The Supreme Court's order of 17 February 2016 in N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016 (Chelameswar and Sapre JJ.), records that on 15 February 2016 'a lot of people gathered including the members of the legal fraternity, students and their supporters and a large number of media persons' and that 'certain unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place in the court premises'. It regulated entry to the court hall for the 2 pm hearing that day: only the lawyers named for the accused, up to four family members, five named journalists, certified by the Registrar General of the Delhi High Court, with no mobile phones, and it directed the Commissioner of Police, Delhi to maintain law and order around the complex.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: On 22 February 2016 the Court corrected the order on the Solicitor General's submission that on 15 February Kanhaiya Kumar 'was not in fact produced before the Patiala House Court Complex but he was only scheduled to be produced there' (see HIST-JNU16-013). The order was issued the morning of 17 February; the order states the Delhi High Court's administrative side was meeting the same day at 2 pm.

claim: The number of people injured at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, and their identities and injuries, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: No source fetched gives a count. Not found: Delhi Police FIR texts (reports say four FIRs were registered over the 15 and 17 February violence), medico-legal certificates (these need the consent of the people concerned), or the aggregate admission figures of any hospital. Routes: RTI to government hospitals for aggregate figures; the FIR copies from Delhi Police; the Delhi Police status report and chargesheets of July 2016 (Metropolitan Magistrate Snigdha Sarvaria, per Legally India).

claim: On 22 February 2016 the Supreme Court corrected its order of 17 February after the Solicitor General said that on 15 February 2016 Kanhaiya Kumar was not in fact produced before the Patiala House Courts Complex but was only scheduled to be produced there.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 22 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: This matters for how the 15 February events are described. The reports read describe the 15 February attack as on students, teachers and journalists, and the attacks on Kanhaiya Kumar himself as on 17 February 2016 (The News Minute, PTI 24 February 2016). Some other outlets, in snippets not read as pages, put an attack on him on 15 February; the court's correction is the better record. The 22 February order also lists the reports then before the Court (HIST-JNU16-015).

claim: The Supreme Court on 17 February 2016 recorded that it deputed six members of the Bar (Kapil Sibal, Rajeev Dhawan, Dushyant Dave, H.P. Rawal, Ajit K. Sinha and A.D.N. Rao) to proceed to Patiala House Courts Complex and report the situation prevailing there, stating 'the presence of the senior advocates might help diffuse the tension'. The order calls them 'the Committee'. It records that the Court had first asked Mr Ajit K. Sinha, 'who represent the Commissioner of Police, Delhi', to obtain the Commissioner's instructions.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: The Committee is a group of advocates deputed by the Court. The group is described in some reports as a 'commission'; the order does not use that word. One member, Mr Sinha, appeared for the Commissioner of Police, Delhi at the same hearing; the order and later orders show him continuing to appear for Delhi Police (for example on 22 February). Reports differ on the size of the team (one PTI report lists seven names for a six-member team); the order lists six.

claim: At about 4 pm on 17 February 2016 the Committee returned and made an oral report; the Supreme Court asked for it in writing. The order records: 'it is reported today by the members of the Committee that the accused was manhandled while he was produced before the Court today', and states 'the responsibility is exclusively is that of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi to ensure the safety of the accused'. The Commissioner of Police, through Mr Sinha, had 'personally assured the safety of the accused and all others who were permitted to attend', and the Court directed him to take necessary steps to ensure the accused's safety until he was next produced.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: The order records only that the accused was manhandled and does not record what the Committee said about police conduct. The office the Court addressed is the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, named by office. The order does not name the person.

claim: The written report of the Supreme Court's Committee of advocates, a pen drive of the video one member recorded on his phone, and other reports were filed in sealed cover. The order of 18 February 2016 records a report by Mr Harin P. Raval on behalf of the Committee, a report from the Delhi High Court's administration, a sealed narrative by one of the accused's counsel, and that the Delhi Police report would follow; it keeps all in sealed cover. The order of 22 February 2016 lists the reports supplied to counsel: Delhi Police's incident report dated 17 February signed by its counsel (given by the Solicitor General), the Bar Council of India's affidavit, the transcription of the video recording and Committee report given by Mr Raval, the report of the accused's counsel, a separate incident report by Mr Ajit Kumar Sinha, and the report of the Registrar General of the Delhi High Court.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 18 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 23 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: The text of the Committee's written report has not been obtained and is not in any document read. The 22 February order also says the Delhi High Court's administrative committee proceedings were not supplied. The 23 February order directs the Registry to mask the Registrar General's identity in copies of the visuals and to verify the pen drive against Mr Raval's phone. Where to look: the Supreme Court registry for the sealed-cover records and any later unsealing, and the Delhi High Court Registrar General's report.

claim: Members of the Supreme Court's Committee told the Court orally on 17 February 2016 that the police did not do their job at Patiala House Courts. PTI reports Mr Dhawan saying that when the accused asked police to stop an intruder, no action was taken, that a man in dark glasses not dressed as a lawyer hit the accused and later sat in the courtroom despite a court order, and that there was a 'serious threat to the life and safety of the accused' which the police would be unable to meet.

sources.originates_from: Oral report of the committee to the Supreme Court, 17 February 2016
Supreme Court committee report, as quoted via LiveLaw

notes: These are statements by Committee members as reported, and allegations from them. The Supreme Court order of the same day records only that the accused was manhandled (HIST-JNU16-015). The News Minute quotes the written report as saying 'the atmosphere outside was surcharged and intimidating' and that there was 'an effort to create an atmosphere of fear and terror', quoted via LiveLaw, and says the report records that Mr Dhawan and Mr Sibal asked police how a person not on the Supreme Court's list could enter the courtroom without a satisfactory reply. The LiveLaw piece (27 January 2018) is an opinion article by a lawyer. The three sources all depend on the same oral and written report and are not independent of it; they are independent of one another as outlets. The 17 February events concern Kanhaiya Kumar's court appearance, not the 15 February attack.

claim: Delhi Police conduct at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, what officers present did or did not do and on whose instructions, is not established by any document read for this file.
notes: The Supreme Court Committee's findings, the NHRC team's findings and the Bar Council affidavit concern mainly 17 February. For 15 February the only primary document read is the Supreme Court order recording that 'unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place'. The Lok Sabha record of 24 February 2016 carries members' statements that police 'stood as a mute spectator' (HIST-JNU16-021), which are members' allegations. A complaint to the NHRC, reproduced in its press release, alleges police 'remained mute spectators' (HIST-JNU16-019). Not found: the Delhi Police report to the Supreme Court (due 19 February 2016), deployment orders and duty rosters for 15 February, station diary or control-room entries, or the Registrar General's report. Routes: RTI to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi and the DCP concerned; the Supreme Court record of the sealed reports; the Delhi High Court Registrar General.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission issued a notice on 17 February 2016 to the Union Home Secretary, the Chief Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police Commissioner on a complaint that journalists and students were beaten outside Patiala House Courts by a Delhi BJP legislator and supporters dressed as lawyers while many police officers 'remained mute spectators', and asked for an urgent report within a week.

sources.publication: National Human Rights Commission, press release of 17 February 2016

notes: VERIFIED as to what the Commission's press release says; the allegations are the complainant's, not a finding. The reply reports are not found. LiveLaw (26 February 2016) says the NHRC report said Kumar was subjected to psychological pressure during questioning and cited serious dereliction of duty by Delhi Police for not preventing the assault or apprehending attackers; this is one secondary report of an NHRC team report, which has not been seen, and is not recorded as established. Obtain the NHRC case file and reply from the Delhi Police Commissioner.

claim: An NHRC fact-finding team report is reported to have found the assault on Kanhaiya Kumar in the court premises 'organized and pre-planned' and to have recorded serious dereliction of duty by Delhi Police.
notes: Reported by LiveLaw on 26 February 2016 as part of a petition's attachments. Other outlets (India TV, Hindustan Times via PressReader) could not be read (403). The NHRC report itself has not been seen. Locate it through the NHRC case record or the petition annexures in the Supreme Court.

claim: The Lok Sabha debated 'the situation arising out of recent incidents in institutions of higher education' on 24 February 2016. The record shows members stating that police stood as 'a mute spectator' while students, teachers and journalists were attacked at Patiala House, and questioning the Home Minister's reliance on a tweet and the Commissioner's public statements; it shows the Minister of Human Resource Development describing the JNU permission slip and the university's own enquiry committee. The record read contains no statement by the Government that names who ordered the police entry onto the JNU campus on 12 February or the police presence at Patiala House on 15 February.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Lok Sabha Debates, 24 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Lok Sabha debates; the Lok Sabha's own copy was not fetched

notes: VERIFIED as to the content of the debate record, which is a primary document. The statements are members' statements, not findings. The record is long (several hundred thousand characters) and was searched for the Home Minister, police, Commissioner, Patiala House, permission and Vice-Chancellor, not read in full. A written reply by the Ministry of Home Affairs to a Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha question on these events was not found; searching sansad.in for starred and unstarred questions of the February to March 2016 sessions is the route.

claim: Delhi Police registered four FIRs over the violence at Patiala House Courts on 15 and 17 February 2016, arrested three lawyers (Vikram Singh Chauhan, Yashpal Singh and Om Sharma) and a Delhi BJP legislator (O.P. Sharma), and released them on bail.
notes: Legally India/IANS (15 May 2016) and The News Minute/PTI (24 February 2016) are different wires. The News Minute reported that as of 24 February Yashpal Singh had been arrested after surrendering at Tilak Marg police station, Om Sharma had been arrested on a Saturday and bailed, and Vikram Singh Chauhan had not responded to notices; the Delhi Police Commissioner is quoted saying police had summoned the lawyers repeatedly and had 'the option of taking coercive action'. The persons named are those the police arrested or charged; no finding of guilt is recorded here. Police took about three months to identify the assailants from CCTV, per Legally India.

claim: Delhi Police filed three chargesheets on 19 July 2016 before Metropolitan Magistrate Snigdha Sarvaria: against three lawyers for the 15 February attack on journalists (rioting, criminal intimidation, causing hurt, mischief); against suspended BJP legislator O.P. Sharma for allegedly assaulting a CPI activist outside the court on 15 February; and against two lawyers for an alleged assault on an advocate inside the complex on 17 February. The assault on Kanhaiya Kumar on 17 February was reported as still under investigation.
notes: Single secondary source (Legally India, from IANS, 23 July 2016); statute numbers are not given. The chargesheets themselves have not been seen. Later outcomes (search snippets, not read as pages, mention an acquittal in October 2021 in a separate case) are not recorded. Obtain the chargesheets and orders from the Patiala House court record.

claim: The Supreme Court on 26 February 2016 issued notice on a petition by advocate Kamini Jaiswal seeking a Special Investigation Team probe into the Patiala House violence of 15 and 17 February and contempt proceedings against three lawyers, with replies sought by the following Friday. A TV sting shown that week was cited in the petition, in which one lawyer was reported to claim that police supported the lawyers.
notes: Single secondary source. Attribution: the statements from the sting are the speakers' claims as reported by LiveLaw ('officers were in uniform, that's why they (too) were not thrashing him'); they are not findings and the footage has not been seen. See HIST-JNU16-025 for a conflicting report of this hearing and HIST-JNU16-026 for the outcome.

claim: India Legal reported on 26 February 2016 that the Supreme Court 'directed the Delhi Police to set up an SIT' to investigate the 15 and 17 February violence; LiveLaw reported on the same day that the Court issued notice on the petition seeking an SIT.
notes: Version 1 (India Legal): the headline and first sentence say the Court directed an SIT, while its body says the petition was 'demanding' one and asks why a fresh petition was filed. Version 2 (LiveLaw): notice only. LiveLaw's later opinion piece (27 January 2018) says the bench of 11 April 2016 orally observed the demand for an SIT was justified and that the plea was dismissed on 24 January 2018. No order text for any of these was read. Neither version is chosen. The Supreme Court orders of 22 February, 23 February, 10 March, 22 and 29 April, 31 August 2016 and 4 May 2017 read for this file are procedural and contain no SIT direction.

claim: The Supreme Court dismissed N.D. Jayaprakash's writ petition (W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016) and a connected contempt petition (Contempt Petition (C) 503/2016) on 14 November 2017, saying 'we find no live issue in the present petitions'. A review petition against the dismissal of the contempt petition, titled N.D. Jayaprakash v. B.S. Bassi, Former Commissioner of Police, Delhi and others, was dismissed on 14 March 2018.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court order of 14 November 2017
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India; the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court order of 14 March 2018 in R.P.(C) 411/2018
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India; the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 31 August 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 4 May 2017
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, 11 September 2017
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy was not fetched

notes: The orders give no reasons beyond 'no live issue'. The title of the review petition names Mr B.S. Bassi, as the Commissioner at the time, as a respondent in the contempt matter; the title shows who the petitioner proceeded against and records no finding about him. The text of the contempt petition's allegations was not read. The 4 May 2017 order sent the matters to a bench of which Justice Chelameswar was not a member; the 31 August 2016 order lists the petitions together. LiveLaw's opinion piece describes a separate dismissal of the SIT plea on 24 January 2018 by a bench of Justices Gogoi and Banumathi quoting 'We don't want to flog a dead horse back into life'; that order was not found or read, so that dismissal is recorded only as a secondary report.

claim: Whether any written authorisation was issued for the police presence at Patiala House Courts Complex on 15 February 2016 and who held command of that deployment is not established by any document read for this file. The only attribution of responsibility in a primary document is the Supreme Court's 17 February 2016 statement that responsibility for the safety of the accused rests exclusively with the Commissioner of Police, Delhi.

sources.publication: Indian Kanoon, reproducing Supreme Court record of proceedings, N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016, 17 February 2016
sources.originates_from: Supreme Court of India daily orders; the court's own copy on sci.gov.in was not fetched

notes: The court's statement is a direction about the office from 17 February onward. It is not a finding about 15 February or about who commanded the earlier deployment. The Wire (Jahnavi Sen, 17 February 2016) reports that although the CRPF had been deployed at the court, Kumar was roughed up and hit on 17 February, and that the Commissioner cited 'jostling' and said there was no option but to take Kumar through the crowd; a single secondary report, not recorded as established. Routes: RTI to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi and the DCP, New Delhi district, for the deployment order and duty rosters; to the CRPF for any requisition; to the Delhi High Court Registrar General for communications with police about security of the complex; and the statutory basis in the Delhi Police Act 1978 for the allocation of command.

claim: JNU wrote to Delhi Police asking them to take utmost precautions before entering the campus, and police officers told the university they would enter only if absolutely necessary under the law and that authorities would be informed in advance.

sources.originates_from: JNU status report to the HRD ministry, as reported

notes: Single secondary source (Onmanorama, 15 February 2016, reporting JNU's status report to the HRD ministry, confirmed by the Registrar per the article). The letter and the report have not been seen. Compare HIST-JNU16-006, which reports a letter giving permission. Both letters are reported and neither has been read.

claim: Police were deployed on the University of Hyderabad campus on 22 March 2016, the day Vice-Chancellor Appa Rao Podile resumed charge after leave following the death of Rohith Vemula, and students and some faculty were removed from the area outside the Vice-Chancellor's lodge and taken into custody that day.
notes: Four independent accounts agree that police were on campus on 22 March and that students were detained that evening. Accounts differ on force used, numbers and cause. No finding on proportionality.

claim: The Registrar's Office notice stated that Prof. Appa Rao Podile 'resumed the charge in the Forenoon of March 22, 2016'.
notes: Quoted in a Round Table India chronology. The notice itself was not read.

claim: Chronology of 22 March 2016 as given by one writer: protesters reached the Vice-Chancellor's residence about 10:30; police arrived about 11:30; RAF and more police arrived about 12:30 and senior officers met the Vice-Chancellor; forcible eviction and lathi-charge began about 16:00; students and three faculty members were taken into custody about 18:00; messes were closed about 21:00.
notes: Single author's account with times given as reported. A student account in the same piece puts police strength at about 400 personnel and four trucks; that figure is unverified.

claim: Count of persons arrested and charged: police and prosecution accounts give 25 students and 2 faculty members (27 accused); the Newslaundry report of the Gachibowli remand diary gives 24 students, 2 faculty members and 1 documentary filmmaker, with 20 more students added to the FIR but not arrested; the Joint Action Committee for Social Justice gave 36 students including 3 professors picked up about 5 pm on 22 March; the Round Table India chronology gives 37 students and 3 faculty members.
notes: Four versions. The 27-accused figure appears at the bail hearing (Sabrang) and in the NHRC release as a media-reported figure. The 36 and 37 figures come from protest groups and a student account and may count people detained and released. The remand diary itself was not read. NHRC gives the arrests as the evening of 23 March; most other sources give 22 March for the detention and 23 March for production in court and remand.

claim: The Joint Action Committee for Social Justice (UoH) alleged that 36 students including 3 professors were detained about 5 pm on 22 March, beaten in a police van and held overnight at undisclosed locations, which it believed to include Miyapur and Narsing police stations.
notes: Allegation by the committee, not a finding. No police or government response appears in the article.

claim: The Independent Fact Finding Team alleged that 27 students and 2 faculty members were taken into police vans, beaten and held in undisclosed locations for more than 24 hours, and alleged beatings, abusive language and threats of rape and death.

sources.publication: Round Table India (republishing the Independent Fact Finding Team press statement, 26 March 2016)

notes: Team members named on the page: Henri Tiphagne, Asha Kowtal, Paul Divakar, Burnard Fatima, V A Ramesh Nathan, Tara Rao (Amnesty International India). Allegations of the team, not findings.

claim: Injuries: PUDR stated that over fifty students were injured; Newslaundry reported a Deputy Commissioner of Police as saying four police officers were injured by stone-pelting; the Round Table India chronology says two students were taken to the health centre at about 11:30 with more hospitalised later.

sources.publication: People's Union for Democratic Rights (press statement, 23 March 2016)

notes: No official injury count, hospital record or medico-legal figure was found. The 'over fifty' figure is PUDR's allegation and its basis is not stated in the statement. Police describe the force used as mild and deny a lathi-charge, as reported by Newslaundry; protest groups describe a lathi-charge.

claim: Police account as reported: after two warnings police used 'mild force'; students allegedly pelted stones, injuring four officers; a lathi-charge and abuse of women students by male police were denied as 'wrongly reported in some media'.
notes: Attributed in the article to a Madhapur Deputy Commissioner of Police. The statement itself was not read. Opposed by the accounts in HIST-HCU-005, 006, 007 and 019.

claim: The Cyberabad Police Commissioner (reported as CV Anand) said of those arrested: 'They were all produced in Miyapur court and sent to judicial remand.'
notes: A statement about what happened after arrest. It does not say who ordered the deployment.

claim: On 28 March 2016 the XXV Metropolitan Magistrate court at Miyapur Court Complex granted bail to 27 accused (reported as 25 students and 2 faculty members), on surety, with a condition to report weekly to the Gachibowli Station House Officer. The public prosecutor did not oppose bail and was quoted as saying the arrests were made 'in order to control the situation'.
notes: Sabrang text is internally inconsistent on the surety amount (Rs 5,000 and Rs 50,000) and on 25 versus 27 students. Sections were described only as damage to public property, trespass, obstructing officials 'and other relevant sections of IPC'. The order and FIR were not read. Countercurrents (HIST-HCU-021) reports bail orders were reserved for 27 persons with hearing on 28 March, consistent with this.

claim: Two cases were registered at Gachibowli police station against protesting students and two faculty members, with charges reported as vandalism, rioting and criminal trespass.
notes: No FIR number, section list or text was found. Search for the FIR and the remand diary is an open task (RTI to Cyberabad Commissionerate, or copy from the Miyapur court).

claim: On 25 March 2016 the National Human Rights Commission took suo motu cognisance of media reports of an 'emergency like situation in Hyderabad University' and issued notices to the Secretary of the Union Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Chief Secretary of Telangana and the Police Commissioner, Hyderabad, seeking reports within one week.

sources.publication: National Human Rights Commission (press release, 25 March 2016)

notes: Primary document read (press release, 25 March 2016). The release records media reports of about 25 students and 2 faculty members arrested on the evening of 23 March, and states 'No one can be deprived of the basic amenities like water, food and electricity by willful act of the State.' It makes no finding on who ordered the police entry. The reports the notices produced were not found.

claim: The replies of the Union HRD Ministry, the Telangana Chief Secretary and the Hyderabad Police Commissioner to the NHRC notice of 25 March 2016, and any NHRC case file number or closure, were not found.
notes: Not located on the NHRC site or in news coverage. Task: NHRC HRCNet case search and RTI to NHRC for the case file.

claim: A writ petition by University of Hyderabad professor Tathagata Sengupta and student P. Adityan led the Hyderabad High Court to direct the Telangana government, in a hearing reported on 19 July 2016, to explain within ten days alleged unlawful police conduct on campus. The advocate said an ACP declined to accept a complaint against a fellow ACP who led the baton charge.
notes: The News Minute gives the campus date as 21 March 2016, which conflicts with 22 March in every other source and is probably an error. The case number, the order and any State counter-affidavit were not found. The article contains no statement from the State on who called the police.

claim: The State's counter-affidavit in the Sengupta and Adityan petition, and any order disposing of it, were not found.
notes: Under SOURCING.md this is the highest-value missing document on the order question. Task: Telangana High Court case status search and Indian Kanoon for the 2016 writ.

claim: Utilities and messes: students said water, electricity and internet were cut and all messes closed from 23 March 2016; a faculty statement says 14 hostel messes were shut for about 48 hours; the Round Table India chronology attributes to the Registrar the words 'Shut down the Messes and the Water facilities, all this protesting students will come to sense'.

sources.publication: Countercurrents.org (statement of SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers, 26 March 2016)
National Human Rights Commission (press release, 25 March 2016)

notes: The students' and faculty claims are allegations. The Registrar quote is an unnamed witness's report. The administration's reported position, seen in search results but not on a page read, is that the water shortage predated the protest and that miscreants damaged a pump. NHRC cites media reports of shortages of water, electricity, food and internet and does not attribute the cause. Who ordered any cut is not established.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The Independent Fact Finding Team interviewed the Cyberabad Deputy Commissioner, an Assistant Commissioner, an Inspector of Police and the Telangana State Home Minister; its published statement and interim report do not record what any of them said about who requested or ordered police entry onto campus.

sources.publication: Round Table India (republishing the Independent Fact Finding Team press statement, 26 March 2016)

notes: The interim report lists the police officer met as a DCP and says a more detailed report will follow. That fuller report was not found. The Vice-Chancellor declined an interview and the team was refused entry to campus.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The fact-finding interim report alleges that the Vice-Chancellor's return to campus was planned with supporters and triggered the violence, and that the Home Minister and police had advised him against returning.
notes: Allegation by the team as summarised by Sabrang. The advice by the Home Minister and police is not documented elsewhere in what was found. This would place a state-government office as having advised against the return, which is different from ordering the entry.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. A Kafila guest post by HCU students states that the CRPF and RAF were 'called in at the behest of the Vice Chancellor Appa Rao'.

sources.publication: Kafila (guest post by HCU students, 23 March 2016)

notes: Student allegation, undated beyond 23 March 2016, with no document cited. Treated as an allegation against the Vice-Chancellor's office.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The Joint Action Committee for Social Justice alleged that police, RAF and CRPF acted 'upon the orders of the Central and state government', and that media reports said police had a list of students and faculty supplied by the Vice-Chancellor.
notes: Allegation without a cited order. The article does not say which media reports. No government response is quoted. The Union government's role is not documented in any source read.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. A faculty statement says security staff 'had been ordered to bar outsiders from entering' the campus, without saying by whom, and that the administration justified the arrests as 'a crack-down on vandals'.

sources.publication: Countercurrents.org (statement of SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers, 26 March 2016)

notes: Statement of the SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers of the University of Hyderabad. Names no officer. Also says Miyapur police told faculty the university lay outside that station's jurisdiction.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The university authorities wrote to Cyberabad police asking it to stop 'media personnel, political groups, external student organisations and politicians' from entering the campus on 22 March 2016.
notes: Newslaundry does not say who signed the letter or whether it was sent before or after police took over the campus. The letter was not seen. This is a request about access by outsiders and is not shown to be a request for police to enter the campus or to detain students.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. An administration 'task sheet' quoted by two University of Hyderabad students in The Wire assigns an administrative officer to inform three named police officers around 08:30 on the day, and to 'request their support if there is any law and order problem'.
notes: The sheet was quoted by the authors and not published; it was not read by this archive. If authentic it shows prior contact planned by the university administration with local police. It does not show who then ordered deployment or detention. The three police officers are named in the article; this entry does not repeat names because the document itself was not read.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The Round Table India chronology reports that non-teaching staff complained to police about students entering the bungalow, while private security gave a different account.
notes: Single source. If a complaint was registered it would be a document (GD entry or complaint copy) obtainable from Gachibowli police station. Not found.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. The public prosecutor told the Miyapur court that 'the arrest were made by the police in order to control the situation' on 22 March.
notes: A court-room statement of the prosecution at the bail hearing as reported by Sabrang. It speaks to the purpose of the arrests, not to who ordered them.

claim: ORDER QUESTION. Who gave the order to bring police and central forces onto the campus and to detain students on 22 March 2016 is not established by any primary document found. No deployment order, requisition, request letter, station diary entry, FIR, affidavit, inquiry report or court order was located naming the office or person.
notes: Candidate offices on the record: the university administration (letter on access to Cyberabad police; task sheet; staff complaint; student allegations), the Cyberabad Police Commissionerate (statements after the fact; the officers on the ground), the Telangana government (Home Minister interviewed by the fact-finding team; alleged advice against the VC's return; NHRC notice to Chief Secretary), and the Union government (alleged by a protest group, CRPF and RAF involvement alleged; no document). None is established.

claim: The Vice-Chancellor had a registered case against him under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in connection with Rohith Vemula's death, on which, according to the fact-finding team, no action had been taken when he returned.
notes: As stated in the interim report. The FIR (Cyberabad, January 2016) was not read. Context for the protest, no finding on its merits.

claim: Procedure after detention: the fact-finding team said those arrested were not produced before a magistrate within 24 hours and that police could have given bail but the students and faculty were remanded; the faculty statement says production at Miyapur court and remand to 14 days' judicial custody followed.

sources.publication: Countercurrents.org (statement of SC and ST Faculty Forum and Concerned Teachers, 26 March 2016)

notes: The Cyberabad Commissioner is reported as saying the accused were produced at Miyapur court and remanded. Whether production met the 24-hour rule depends on the time of arrest, which sources put at about 17:00 to 18:00 on 22 March, with remand late on 23 March. The remand order and arrest memos were not read.

claim: Police used force, including a lathicharge, against protesting students at Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi, on the night of 23 September 2017. Press reports say women students, at least two journalists and some police personnel were injured.
notes: Occurrence is consistent across sources. The Vice-Chancellor denied that students were lathicharged on campus (see HIST-BHU-012). Location of the force (campus gates, women's hostel area, outside campus) differs between accounts and is not resolved here.

claim: Students began protesting at BHU after 21 September 2017, when a woman student said she was harassed by three men on a motorcycle inside the campus. Students alleged that when she complained at the Proctor's office she was shamed and told not to go out after 6 pm. The allegation about the Proctor's office is the students' and is not a finding.
notes: Newslaundry gives the 21 September timeline; Outlook describes the harassment allegation. Neither shows a document from the university.

claim: The Varanasi Divisional Commissioner submitted a report to the Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary on or about 26 September 2017. As reported by IANS, it said BHU did not deal with the victim's complaint in a sensitive manner or in time, and called the administration's failure 'the biggest fault'. The reports do not say the report examined who ordered the police action.
notes: The report itself was not found or read. The three outlets relay the same findings; IANS appears to be the common origin, so these are not three independent sources. Chief Minister asked for this report on 24 or 25 September (see HIST-BHU-009).

claim: Who gave the order for the lathicharge on the night of 23 September 2017 is not established in any document or report retrieved. No order, police log, magistrate's direction or inquiry finding naming the office that authorised the use of force was found.
notes: Sources read are silent on the point: Outlook (25 and 26 September 2017), Newslaundry, The Quint, National Herald, Tribune. Documents that would settle it: Varanasi district magistrate's and police commissionerate or SSP's records of the deployment and any direction to disperse, Lanka police station general diary, the magisterial inquiry report, the state judicial inquiry report, and BHU's record of any request for police help. The BHU spokesperson was reported saying 'police help had been sought' (Outlook, 25 September 2017) without saying who sought it or from whom.

claim: On 24 September 2017 journalists protesting in Lucknow demanded action against the Varanasi District Magistrate and the Senior Superintendent of Police 'for ordering the lathicharge'. This is the journalists' allegation as reported. The same report describes the two officers meeting university officers and does not say they ordered anything.
notes: Single source, and it attributes the order only through the protesters' demand. The offices (District Magistrate, SSP) are named in the source with individual names; those names are omitted here because no primary document was read that ties them to the order. Not a finding.

claim: Between 24 and 25 September 2017 the Varanasi district administration and police removed from their posts three additional city magistrates, the station officer of Lanka police station and the circle officer of Bhelupur, reported as 'in connection with the lathicharge'. Dynamite News and Aaj Tak say the officials were found prima facie responsible for the lathicharge. The reports do not name the authority that issued the removal order.
notes: Outlook reproduces a district information office release for the magistrates and police sources for the police officers. The release was not itself read. Reports differ on numbers: Aaj Tak and Dynamite list one additional city magistrate, the Lanka station officer and the Bhelupur circle officer; Outlook lists three magistrates (see HIST-BHU-007). A removal is an administrative step and is not a finding that any of them gave the order.

claim: Reports differ on how many officials were removed. Outlook (25 September 2017) lists three additional city magistrates plus the Lanka station officer and the Bhelupur circle officer. Aaj Tak (25 September 2017) lists one additional city magistrate plus those two police officers. The Tribune (27 September 2017) says three additional city magistrates and three policemen. Outlook's 26 September piece says two police officers.
notes: Versions kept side by side. Resolution needs the district information office release or the government order itself.

claim: Police registered an FIR against unidentified policemen over the lathicharge of 23 September 2017 and a separate case against over 1,000 students over the violence, announced on 25 September 2017 at Lanka police station per PTI.
notes: FIR texts, sections and complainants were not found. PTI is the common origin of both outlets.

claim: The number of students named in the case differs between reports: over 1,000 (PTI via Outlook and Eastern Mirror, 25 September 2017) and 1,200 unidentified students (Aaj Tak, 25 September 2017).
notes: Only the FIR would settle the figure.

claim: The number of people injured on 23 September 2017 is not established. Reports say only 'a number of students, including women, and two journalists' were injured, and that some police personnel were hurt per police sources. No source retrieved gives a count.
notes: Hospital admission and medico-legal figures were not found. Consent and privacy limits apply to individual medical records; aggregate hospital figures could be sought by RTI.

claim: Detentions reported: 16 detained students were released on the evening of 24 September 2017, per the Lanka station officer quoted by PTI via Outlook. Over 200 Samajwadi Party activists were detained while trying to reach the injured students, and Congress leaders were detained and later released while heading to BHU. No total number of students detained on the night of 23 September is given.
notes: Several of these detentions are of political workers on 24 and 25 September, not of students on the night of the lathicharge.

claim: Vice-Chancellor Girish Chandra Tripathi denied, as reported on 26 September 2017, that students were lathicharged on campus. He said action was taken against people who threw petrol bombs and stones and tried to burn property, and that police used force only to move such elements out of the campus. He also described the protest as created by outsiders and said it was staged before the Prime Minister's visit. These are his statements as reported.
notes: Statements attributed to the Vice-Chancellor by IANS, NDTV (via National Herald) and Outlook. They do not say who ordered the police to act.

claim: On 24 and 25 September 2017 the Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister ordered a probe and sought a report from the Divisional Commissioner, Varanasi; the Varanasi district administration ordered a magisterial inquiry into the four days of incidents including the lathicharge; and a state judicial inquiry was announced. Outlook also reports a committee under the Chief Secretary.
notes: The orders constituting these inquiries were not read. Outcomes of the magisterial and state judicial inquiries were not found.

claim: The BHU Vice-Chancellor ordered a judicial inquiry led by a retired Allahabad High Court judge, reported on 26 September 2017 after an executive council meeting. The judge's name is given as V K Dixit by The Tribune and Morung Express and as B S Dixit by Outlook.
notes: Judge's name differs across sources; the order was not read. This is a university inquiry, separate from the state's.

claim: The BHU inquiry committee headed by a former High Court judge released its findings on 25 April 2018, per The Wire's LiveWire. It is reported to have given the Vice-Chancellor a clean chit and to have described the protest as 'politicised and sponsored'.
notes: Single source and an opinion-leaning piece. The report text was not found. Not read for what it says about who ordered the police action. Treat as unverified until the report is obtained.

claim: BHU Chief Proctor O N Singh resigned on 26 September 2017, reported as taking 'moral responsibility' for the molestation of a student and the police violence that followed. The Tribune attributes no direct quote to him.
notes: Resignation is reported as a fact; the reason is the press's description. No document names the Proctor as having requested or ordered police action.

claim: Vice-Chancellor Tripathi went on leave on 2 October 2017 citing personal reasons, and the BHU registrar was appointed interim Vice-Chancellor on 4 October 2017, per The Quint's live blog.
notes: Single dated source.

claim: The National Human Rights Commission sought a detailed report on the incident from the Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary, the Director General of Police and the Vice-Chancellor within four weeks, per The Quint.
notes: NHRC case number and notice were not found. Replies, if filed, would be primary evidence on the chain of command.

claim: Aaj Tak reports (25 September 2017) that the Prime Minister and the BJP president spoke to the Chief Minister and asked him to take necessary steps. Outlook says 'reportedly'. This is a press account of a conversation and is not a direction about the lathicharge.
notes: Sourcing of the conversation is not given in either article.

claim: No Allahabad High Court order, petition or commission report on the BHU events of 21 to 24 September 2017 was found in this research.
notes: Searches of news coverage returned no High Court proceeding. Indian Kanoon and the eCourts portal were not searched in this pass and should be before concluding no case exists. The only judge-led inquiry found is the university's (HIST-BHU-014).

claim: Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel entered the Jamia Millia Islamia campus in the evening of 15 December 2019 and used force and tear gas there. The Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 records, from the NHRC's findings, that protesters pushed back by police entered the campus 'following which the police also entered the campus' (para 81), and that the use of tear-gas shells inside the library 'could have been avoided' (paras 18, 42, 83).

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020

notes: The occurrence is established by a court judgment that recites the NHRC's findings and by the police's own account to a magistrate (secondary report of the action taken report). The court makes no finding that any individual officer acted unlawfully and says its conclusion is not an approval of every act attributed to police (para 92). Time of entry is DISPUTED between sources: the petitioners' case in the judgment (para 12) says about 4:00 p.m.; Wikipedia (tertiary, not independently checked) says 6:46 p.m. The judgment does not fix a time.

claim: On 13 December 2019 a march by Jamia students towards Parliament was stopped near the campus. The petitioners' case, as recited in the Delhi High Court judgment, is that at about 3:00 p.m. police resorted to tear-gas shelling in the vicinity of the campus and several students were injured. LiveLaw's account of the NHRC report says the 13 December 'clash' was contained at Gate No. 1 and that no complaint was made to any authority about it.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: The judgment (para 11) states this as the petitioners' case, not as a finding. Wikipedia (tertiary) says 50 students were detained on 13 December; that count was not checked against its cited news sources and is not repeated as established. No document read here says who gave any order on 13 December. The 13 December events are far less documented than 15 December.

claim: Who gave the order to enter the campus on 15 December 2019: NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read for this record names the person or the office that ordered the entry. The Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 describes the entry as an act of 'the police' and names no officer or rank. The police's action taken report (16 March 2020), as reported by Scroll.in and The Quint, says police were 'forced to enter' and names no officer. The Home Ministry's written Lok Sabha reply of 4 February 2020, as reported by The Leaflet, says police entered 'chasing the violent congregation of students/ mob' and names no officer.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
Written reply by MoS (Home) G. Kishan Reddy in the Lok Sabha, reported 4 February 2020

notes: Level of office: the only institution all sources attribute the entry to is the Delhi Police (with Rapid Action Force personnel, para 18 of the judgment). The rank at which the decision was taken (station, district, range, headquarters, or the Union Home Ministry, to which Delhi Police reports) is unknown. The judgment records no police counter-affidavit statement naming a commander. The NHRC report (read only through summaries) is also reported as naming no one. The Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southeast) is named in a Scroll.in report only as an official who declined to comment on the firing inquiry; no document says he gave any order and this archive makes no such claim. Documents that could settle it are listed at HIST-JMI-020 to HIST-JMI-023.

claim: Who gave the order to use tear gas, including inside the library: NOT ESTABLISHED. The Delhi Police action taken report, as reported, says officials 'used tear gas shells and moderate force to disperse the protestors' and names no authorising officer. The NHRC found, as recorded in the Delhi High Court judgment, that the use of tear-gas shells inside the library 'could have been avoided'. LiveLaw's and The Wire's summaries of the NHRC report say it called the tear gas 'an irresponsible action of the police' and recommended action against those who used it.

sources.publication: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 in W.P.(C) 13468/2019 and connected matters, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police action taken report filed in a Delhi magistrate's court, 16 March 2020
NHRC report, as summarised by The Wire on 26 June 2020 (the report itself was not read)
NHRC report, as summarised by LiveLaw on 27 June 2020 (the report itself was not read)

notes: The NHRC recommendation of action against personnel who used tear gas in the library is reported by two outlets, but the report itself was not read and no action against any identified officer has been found (see HIST-JMI-018). Whether the tear gas was fired on an order from a supervisor or on individual decision is not stated in any document read.

claim: Who gave the order to use lathis or other force against students, and who ordered detentions: NOT ESTABLISHED. The Delhi Police action taken report, as reported, says students were 'temporarily apprehended' under section 65 of the Delhi Police Act and evacuated 'hands up'. The police's June 2020 affidavit in the High Court, as reported by The Quint, says 'No student was ever arrested or detained either in the police lock up or otherwise at that time' and that apprehended students were handed to a proctor. No document read names an officer or office that ordered either.

The case diary holding the statements was reportedly not yet with the Crime Branch SIT at that date.

claim: Jamia's Vice-Chancellor, Najma Akhtar, said on 16 December 2019: 'Police entered the campus without permission.' The Chief Proctor, Waseem Ahmed Khan, is reported to have said the same. The Delhi High Court judgment records that the petitioners rely on the Chief Proctor's statement that no permission was sought (para 31) and quotes a social media post attributed to him (para 13). On 19 December 2019 senior advocate Indira Jaising told the High Court that 'neither the VC nor Proctor granted permission to Delhi Police to enter the campus'.

notes: This corroborates that the university said permission was not given. No document read shows police asking for or being refused permission, or a police statement either way. The NHRC, as summarised by The Leaflet, also recorded that the university administration showed 'abject failure' in communication with police.

claim: The Delhi Police position is that entry was necessary. June 2020 affidavit, as reported by The Quint: entry was 'imperative' because the university was 'used as a shield by rioters'; brutality allegations were an 'utter falsehood'. Home Ministry written Lok Sabha reply of 4 February 2020, as reported: police 'entered the University Campus chasing the violent congregation of students/ mob'.

Maktoob reports the magistrate, Rajat Goyal, held the police acts fell within official duties while acknowledging police 'may have exceeded' their jurisdiction and could have shown more restraint. The Delhi High Court records that this order was unchallenged and 'attained finality' (paras 19, 45).

The Delhi High Court judgment (paras 17, 18) records complaints about 34 detained students, the Commission's team visiting on 20 December 2019, a further complaint on 16 January 2020 with statements of 91 students, and a report dated 18 May 2020.

claim: Delhi High Court judgment of 5 October 2026 (Justices Vivek Chaudhary and Manoj Jain; reserved 24 July 2026) dismissed the batch of eight writ petitions (lead: W.P.(C) 13468/2019; includes W.P.(Crl) 3522/2019, Nabila Hasan v. Union of India). It declined an independent judicial commission, SIT or fact-finding body, declined compensation, declined fresh guidelines for police entry into campuses, and found no direction on CCTV preservation necessary because the State had stated on affidavit (5 May 2023) that all footage was preserved and part of the charge-sheets. It left individuals free to pursue other remedies.

claim: Police and paramilitary personnel (Rapid Action Force) entered the Aligarh Muslim University campus on the evening and night of 15 December 2019 during an anti-Citizenship Amendment Act protest, and used force including tear gas.
notes: Occurrence is not in dispute between the petitioner, the State and the University. What force was used is contested: the State's counter affidavit, as reported, says water cannons and tear gas were used and no lethal weapon; students allege rubber bullets, pellets and stun grenades. See HIST-AMU-006. No finding on proportionality.

claim: The Registrar of Aligarh Muslim University issued a notice on 15 or 16 December 2019 closing the university until 5 January 2020 and asking students to vacate hostels.
notes: The Caravan interview (31 December 2019) says the university was closed until 5 January. A search summary, not a fetched page, attributed a closure notice to Registrar Abdul Hamid citing 'disturbances created by certain anti-social elements'; that attribution is unverified. SCC Online Times reports the petitioner's account that notices to vacate hostels were issued on 16 December 2019. The notice itself was not seen. Date of the notice varies by source.

claim: Internet services in Aligarh were suspended from 10 pm on 15 December 2019 to 10 pm on 16 December 2019, on the order of the District Magistrate of Aligarh, Chandra Bhushan Singh, according to news reports. The stated reason was that anti-social elements could use internet services to spread inflammatory content on social media.
notes: OFFICE-LEVEL ANSWER: District Magistrate, Aligarh. ETV Bharat (16 December 2019) names DM Chandra Bhushan Singh; WION (22 December 2019) says the District Magistrate ordered it and quotes him that services stay suspended 'from 10 pm tonight till 10 pm tomorrow'. The order itself was not seen, so its legal basis (statute and rules invoked) and any confirmation by the state Home Department are not established. Name given by one outlet only; both outlets attribute to the DM. Both are news reports of a statement, not a primary document. The shutdown tracker internetshutdowns.in lists the same hours and classes it as mobile, citing News18, but its entry is dated 14 December 2019 on its face, which is before the event; treated as unreliable for date and not used for confidence.

claim: The State of Uttar Pradesh's counter affidavit in the Allahabad High Court, filed for the Inspector General (Law and Order) and the SSP Aligarh, as reported, states that students gathered at University Circle in breach of Section 144 CrPC, that the University Registrar asked the District Magistrate to take appropriate steps and sent a letter requesting security deployment, that the district administration had intelligence inputs and information from the University Proctor about a march towards Bab-e-Syed, and that stone pelting in the dark damaged property so the administration entered the campus to disperse the crowd.
notes: OFFICE-LEVEL ANSWER (State's account): the State says the district administration entered the campus after a request from the University Registrar. It attributes the decision to 'the administration', not to a named officer. The affidavit was not read; this is SCC Online Times' summary of the January 2020 order (Mohd. Aman Khan v. Union of India, Criminal Misc. PIL/Petition No. 26085 of 2019). Sabrang's report confirms the affidavit was filed for the IG (Law and Order) and the SSP and that it alleges breach of Section 144, but did not state the Registrar-letter detail in the text fetched. An allegation by the State, attributed to it.

claim: The Vice Chancellor of AMU, Tariq Mansoor, said publicly that the administration was 'left with no other choice but to call the police' and that the decision was 'timely and necessary'. Separately the University told the High Court, as reported, that police entered 'being called by the University authorities'.
notes: OFFICE-LEVEL ANSWER (University's account): the University administration says it called the police. The Quint (25 December 2019, updated 6 January 2020) quotes the Vice Chancellor; The Leaflet reports the University's position as 'being called by the University authorities'. The written request or letter was not seen. Contested by the AMU Students' Union president, who told The Caravan (31 December 2019) that the Vice Chancellor and Registrar had accepted giving written permission for police to enter and use 'appropriate force'; this is a claim by the student leader and is not independently confirmed in that article. The Karwan e Mohabbat fact-finding report (17 December 2019 visit) records that the Vice Chancellor claims to have invited the forces, says the Registrar, Proctor and Vice Chancellor cited stone throwing, and states the team suspected the invitation papers may have been signed after entry, which it said needs verification. That is the report's suspicion, not a finding. Scroll.in reports that AMU said police entered a hostel without permission, which is a separate point from the call for police. Who inside the University signed is not established. Timing of the request relative to entry is not established.

claim: Counts disputed.
