Injured: about 70 students injured per PTI-based reports, 40 to 50 seen by a professor in hospital, about 100 injured and about 100 picked up per teachers and doctors cited in the Karwan e Mohabbat report, and police and RAF personnel also injured per the SSP. The High Court later referred to six students as grievously injured.

claim: The NHRC findings, as reported, do not state who gave the order for police entry, for use of force, for the internet suspension or for Section 144. The orders and recommendations reported are addressed to the DGP, CRPF DG, Chief Secretary and AMU's Vice Chancellor and Registrar. No magisterial inquiry into the 15 December 2019 events was found in any source read.
notes: This is a record of absence in secondary summaries, not of the NHRC report itself, which was not obtained. A magisterial inquiry may exist and was not found; absence of a hit is not proof. Next steps: RTI to NHRC for its report (case reference from the High Court order); RTI to the District Magistrate and Home Department UP for any inquiry notification, the Section 144 order and the internet suspension order.

claim: The Registrar of AMU is described in the Karwan e Mohabbat fact-finding report as a serving Uttar Pradesh police officer on deputation. The report also says the Proctor reportedly told doctors not to send University ambulances.

The report's footnote says responsibility for errors lies with Harsh Mander. Allegations as the report made them; not tested. The Registrar's name (Abdul Hamid) appeared only in a search summary and is not confirmed from a fetched page. That is the report's statement; no source for it was shown on the page.

Both versions are as reported; the affidavit text was not seen. Karwan e Mohabbat report says the Registrar confirmed use of stun grenades, tear gas and water cannons. Allegations by students are attributed to them.

claim: On 5 January 2020 a group of masked people armed with sticks and rods entered the Jawaharlal Nehru University campus, New Delhi, and attacked students and teachers over roughly two to three hours from about 6.30 to 7 pm. Whether they were stopped or arrested is covered in separate records.
notes: Occurrence corroborated. Duration differs by source (nearly two hours in the Tribune report of 6 January 2020, three hours in NDTV's). No finding on who the attackers were; attributions in the press are allegations by students, the ABVP and others and are not recorded here.

claim: Injury count on 5 January 2020 differs by source: at least 34 (NDTV, 6 January 2020); about 35 (ETV Bharat, 9 January 2020); at least 32 students (Al Jazeera, 7 January 2020); 28 students and a teacher (National Herald on a Rajya Sabha reply, 18 March 2020); 36 students, teachers and staff (SabrangIndia, 2021); 51 persons, per a Lok Sabha written reply by the Minister of State for Home as reported by Delhi Police (National Herald, February 2020). No deaths are reported.

sources.originates_from: Lok Sabha written reply by MoS Home G. Kishan Reddy, reported by National Herald; the reply itself was not retrieved

notes: Both versions kept. The 51 figure rests on a ministerial reply the archive has not read. Ask for the Lok Sabha question and answer text on sansad.in to settle which count the Government gave and on which date. The counts may measure different things (admitted to hospital, medically examined, treated and discharged).

claim: A Delhi Police spokesperson, Mandeep Singh Randhawa, said on 6 January 2020 that police 'can go to this area only with a written permission from the JNU administration' and that 'Police initiated action only after permission was received.' The committee was a self-review by the force and its clean chit is an internal finding.

National Herald reported on 5 January 2020 that police 'waited outside varsity gates saying they didn't have the permission from the Vice Chancellor or Registrar to enter inside', and entered around 9 pm. notes: The RTI replies are cited only through Wikipedia and are not confirmed. The Wire, News18 and NDTV articles that Wikipedia cites were not read (The Wire page returned headline only; NDTV and News18 not fetched). The gate footage question bears directly on who was at the gates.

notes: Single source, anonymous. It shows police already had a working channel to the registrar, relevant to who communicated with whom. The letters were not seen.

claim: On 5 January 2020 the Delhi Police presence on campus before the attack: Delhi Police said a team including an inspector was deployed at the administrative block (about 27 personnel from 8 am, per the committee report as relayed) to enforce a Delhi High Court order barring protests within 100 metres, and that those personnel were unarmed.

claim: Who gave the order that police would or would not enter the JNU campus, or hold at the gates, on 5 January 2020: no order, written or oral, and no named person who gave one has been found in any document the archive has read. The record shows only (a) the police statement that written permission from the university was required and arrived at 7.45 pm from the Registrar, (b) the university's statement that it called police at about 4.30 pm, (c) the Home Ministry's statement that police deployed inside after the Vice-Chancellor requested help, and (d) a Times of India report that constables were told to avoid confrontation and wait for orders, with no issuing office named.
notes: UNKNOWN is the correct state. Not established: who decided that police would wait; whether any police officer (DCP South-West, SHO, Commissioner) issued an instruction to hold; whether the Ministry of Home Affairs, which oversees Delhi Police, was consulted before the attack (the Times of India reports the Union Home Minister asked for a report on 6 January 2020, after the attack); the content of the VC's WhatsApp message and the Registrar's letter; and the legal position that a university's consent is required before police enter, which a lawyer should confirm against current law.

claim: Whether a charge sheet has been filed against anyone in the Crime Branch investigation into the 5 January 2020 JNU violence, and the current status of the three cases: not found. The latest source read is the 3 August 2021 Lok Sabha reply (no arrests, SIT constituted).
notes: Searches for later coverage and court records found nothing after mid-2020 other than the 2021 reply. File an RTI with the Crime Branch and check the Patiala House eCourts record.

IANS

claim: On 9 December 2015 students marching from the UGC protest toward Parliament were stopped near Feroz Shah Road. Police used lathis, water cannon and tear gas, and detained students for several hours. The News Minute reports 150 detained, all later released, and several injured.

sources.originates_from: Reporter who was himself detained
Quotes Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) as reported by the Indian Express; that report was not itself read

Caravan puts the number of marchers at over 300 and says detainees were held at or near Parliament Street; Sabrang says three buses took students to Parliament Street police station. No source gives an injury count. Scroll reports that at the time the protest was in its 51st day. This episode is outside the date range given for the incident and is recorded because it concerns the same protest.

claim: The reasons for force on 9 December 2015 are DISPUTED. The Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) said force was used to stop a march toward Parliament, that the approved route ran from ITO via Barakhamba Road to Jantar Mantar, and that protesters turned violent and attacked police at the Le Meridien roundabout. Students and AISA's national president said the march was peaceful. Scroll describes a video it says shows no stone-pelting.

Reporter who was himself detained

claim: On 9 December 2015 a police officer at the cordon told Caravan's reporter, 'We have orders from above. No one from inside goes out and no one from outside gets in.' The officer wore no name badge and declined to give his name.

sources.originates_from: Reporter who was himself detained

claim: Who gave the order for the October 2015 detentions near the UGC office, and for any force used on 21 to 27 October, is not established. No document read names an issuing officer or office. notes: At the level of office, the candidates are the Delhi Police district whose area includes the UGC office and the police station with jurisdiction, but no page read says so and this is not asserted. Delhi Police reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is the route for an RTI. Do not name any individual as the giver of an order on this record.

claim: Who gave the order for the 9 December 2015 force and detentions is not established. The deputy commissioner of police (New Delhi) publicly defended the use of force, and an unnamed officer cited 'orders from above', but no document names who authorised it.

claim: Whether any prohibitory order under the criminal procedure code (Section 144 of the old code, or its successor) was in force near the UGC office in October 2015 is not established. No source read mentions one for the UGC office.
notes: Several searches for a prohibitory order tied to the UGC office returned nothing. The only Section 144 result was an unrelated protest. Delhi Police issue such orders by notification; whether one existed would be shown by a Delhi Police or Delhi government notification, which was not found.

claim: PUDR wrote to the chairperson of the Delhi Commission for Women on 14 December 2015 asking for an inquiry into allegations of molestation and sexual assault by Delhi Police against women students at the 9 December 2015 march, and for action against those found responsible. claim: Records that could be requested to answer who gave the order: Delhi Police daily diary entries for the police stations with jurisdiction over the UGC office and for Bhalswa, Kamla Market and Parliament Street stations on 21 to 27 October and 9 December 2015; deployment orders and bandobast instructions; any Section 144 notification; the detention lists and release memos for each station; the DCP (Central) and DCP (New Delhi) reports to headquarters; any Ministry of Home Affairs correspondence; and any reply by the Delhi Commission for Women to PUDR's letter.

claim: Police cleared the Marina Beach protest camp in Chennai on the morning of 23 January 2017 using force, including batons and, in some reports, tear gas, on protesters who had gathered since mid-January against the ban on Jallikattu. The Tribune's agency report says police 'fired teargas shells and resorted to lathicharge to disperse crowds' on that day in Chennai and other cities. Police told PTI they used 'mild force' after protesters threw sand and water packets; a protester told PTI police used tear gas and batons.

sources.publication: Gulf News (PTI report; page last updated 1 November 2018)
sources.originates_from: PTI, 23 January 2017
Own reporting; says police 'forcibly evicted protesters from agitation sites across the state' on 23 January 2017

notes: Occurrence of force corroborated by three secondary outlets plus a tertiary summary. The reports are not independent of each other on detail: Gulf News carries a PTI account and the Tribune item is an agency dateline. No finding on proportionality, provocation or lawfulness. Police and protester accounts differ on whether tear gas was fired (a protester says yes, police say 'mild force'); the Tribune says tear gas shells were fired.

claim: Many of the Marina protesters were students and young people. The Tribune report records that the 'students and youth who had called the protest' say they were not involved in the violence that followed; the Wikipedia article records that on 24 January 2017 students called off their protest after talks with police and a district judge; The Federal describes most of those later charged as 'youngsters'; the one-man inquiry commission invited 'people and students' to depose. The protest was broad and not made up only of students.
notes: Included to fix the scope: this record is about a youth-led, student-heavy protest, and no source read gives a count of students among those removed or charged. Do not read it as a purely student event. Confidence is REPORTED because no source states the share of students.

claim: Injury figures for 23 January 2017 differ. Gulf News (PTI) says at least 20 people were injured in clashes with police. Wikipedia says 'around 60 people, including 33 policemen' were admitted to state-run hospitals. The Tribune says only that 'a number of policemen and members of the public were also injured'. No source read breaks the figures down into protesters and police for Marina alone, and none cites a hospital record.

sources.originates_from: PTI, 23 January 2017

notes: The figures may measure different things (Marina only against statewide, injured against admitted), so they are listed side by side rather than reconciled. Hospital admission registers and police casualty reports would settle it.

claim: Number removed or detained on 23 January 2017 at Marina: NOT ESTABLISHED. claim: Who gave the order to clear Marina Beach on 23 January 2017, and in what form (written or oral): NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read names an officer or office as the source of the order. Pages read that are silent on it: Tribune (23 January 2017), Gulf News/PTI, Deccan Chronicle (17 February 2017), The Federal (14 January 2021), Sri Lanka Guardian (22 January 2025), the Madras High Court judgment of 28 April 2018, and Wikipedia.
notes: Recorded at the level of office: the police operation in Chennai falls within the Greater Chennai Police, whose head is the Commissioner of Police (the office the High Court judgment records as issuing the later section 144 order). The Chief Minister is reported by two outlets to have defended the operation in the Assembly (see HIST-C17A-009); a defence after the event is not an order. People's Watch states that the Commissioner declined to meet its fact-finding team; that is not an attribution of the order.

claim: On 21 February 2017 a seminar titled 'Cultures of Protest', organised by the English Department at Ramjas College, University of Delhi, was disrupted by ABVP supporters who objected to the invitation to JNU student Umar Khalid, and the college administration cancelled it. Newslaundry reports ABVP supporters allegedly threw bricks into the seminar room and that Khalid, advised by police stationed at the college not to attend, did not come. The Quint reports the college withdrew the invitation to Khalid and Shehla Rashid after ABVP opposed it.

The Wikipedia background section (tertiary, citing The Wire) says the principal and a professor tried to reason with the protesters, that police formed a cordon to let attendees into the venue, and that a mob pelted them with stones; that text was read but is not counted as a corroborating source because it is a summary of one cited article. The Wire article was not read.

claim: On 22 February 2017 AISA students and teachers at Ramjas College set out to march to Maurice Nagar police station (not a 'Kamla Nagar' station; no source read uses that name) to demand action over the previous day. claim: Delhi Police detained students on 22 February 2017 near Maurice Nagar police station. claim: On 20 September 2018 a protest by students and parents against the posting of Urdu and Sanskrit teachers at Darivit High School, Islampur block, Uttar Dinajpur district, West Bengal, ended in a confrontation with police in which two young men, Tapas Barman and Rajesh Sarkar, died of gunshot injuries. The Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 records the event as the subject of FIR No. 611 of 2018 (paras 1 to 4) and orders compensation to the families of those 'killed and injured' (para 77). The court does not find who fired the shots.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The two deaths are named in the judgment (paras 4, 12), which is the document this archive relies on for the names. Ages differ: Indian Express and Hindustan Times (2018) give 19 and 21 for the two. The judgment calls the dead 'boys' and 'students' in the NHRC extract and does not give ages. Whether either was a minor is not established here. Both are described by the press as former students of the school. Indian Express (20 September 2018) first reported one death; the second death was reported the next day (HT, 23 September 2018: one died 'on the spot', the other 'on Friday').

claim: Police used tear gas and rubber bullets at Darivit High School on 20 September 2018. This is stated by the police themselves: the High Court records the gist of the police FIR as saying 'The police too fired tear gas and rubber bullets' (para 4), and the Superintendent of Police of the district was quoted on the day saying 'We have fired rubber bullets and tear gas shells. We did not fire bullets.'

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The SP's quotation is from The Indian Express, 20 September 2018, and is a newspaper's report of a spoken statement. The FIR account is a primary document as recited by the court (the FIR itself was not read). The same sources attribute the first use of force to a mob attacking the police. That attribution is the police version and is not found by the court.

claim: Whether police use of force on 20 September 2018 was excessive, and what it included, is DISPUTED. (a) Police and State version: police were 'suddenly attacked by an unruly mob with bricks, lathi, bombs, and firearms' (FIR gist, para 4) and the CID report is 'the actual sequence of events' (State counsel, para 28). (b) NHRC version, quoted in the judgment (para 25, conclusion iii): 'The police action seems to have used excessive force (lathi charge, tear gas, rubber bullets) without any warning and landed up beating students, misbehavior with girl students'. The State argued that no complainant or petitioner alleged molestation of girl students and that the complainants did not come forward to depose (para 42). The court did not make its own finding on molestation; it accepted the NHRC report only 'as a preliminary inquiry finding' (para 58) and listed among the NHRC findings that police 'may have used excessive force to break through the students and enter the school' (para 59(c)). Indian Express (20 September 2018) reported that police resorted to lathi charge 'as the students lobbed bricks and stones'.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: No finding of guilt or intent is made here. The NHRC report itself was not read; only the extracts quoted in the judgment. The judgment says the NHRC report 'may be without jurisdiction and cannot technically or legally be called a statutory report' (para 47) because the State Human Rights Commission had taken cognisance first, and the State asked the court to ignore it entirely (para 29).

claim: Who fired the bullets that killed two men is DISPUTED. (a) Police and State: police deny firing bullets (SP quoted in Indian Express, 20 September 2018, and Hindustan Times, 23 September 2018); the State told the court 'The police were not responsible for the firing' (para 28); the FIR names bullet injuries as caused in an attack on police by a mob with firearms (para 4); the CID theory is that a person in the mob fired. The Chief Minister said police did not open fire (NDTV, 23 September 2018). (b) Families and the NHRC: the NHRC conclusion quoted at para 25 says villagers 'unambiguously alleged that the last police vehicle had fired', and that the autopsy analysis was 'suggestive of use of rifled weapon fired from a short range and may be from a slight height (may be aboard a vehicle as alleged)'. (c) The court: it found the CID theory that a person in the mob fired 'incredible' (para 61(f)) and recorded 'a strong possibility that bullets had been fired from the last police vehicle leaving the place of occurrence' as a point drawn from one injured person's statement to the NHRC (para 61(h)). It also records that the State told the court the CID 'could not arrive at any conclusion as regards the firing of the bullets and the weapon used therefor' (para 41).

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)
The Indian Express (Express News Service), 20 September 2018

notes: The court's statements are made in deciding to transfer the investigation and are described by the court as reasons to doubt the CID's work, not as a trial finding on who fired. Nobody has been convicted or charged on the court's reading in the documents read. The weapon, and who held it, are not established in any document read.

claim: Who gave the order for police to go to Darivit High School, to enter or break through to the school gate, and to use lathis, tear gas and rubber bullets: NOT ESTABLISHED. No document read names the person or the office that gave any of these orders. The judgment records the FIR account that police received information at 2.05 pm (GD entry No. 875), that the Inspector-in-Charge of Islampur police station, with a contingent of additional officers and police force, reached the school (para 3), and the NHRC's extract that the police 'were ill equipped' at first and that 'Reinforcements were later called by the police' (para 25, iii) without saying who called them.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: Level of office: the only rank the judgment places at the scene is the Inspector-in-Charge of the police station, as the FIR's own account. Whether the Sub-Divisional Police Officer, the Superintendent of Police or the District Magistrate was present or gave any direction is not stated in any document read. The Indian Express (20 September 2018) quotes the District Magistrate as saying he was 'waiting for the police report' and the SP as saying police 'have fired rubber bullets and tear gas shells', and says nothing about who ordered either. Documents that could settle it are listed at HIST-DAR-014 and HIST-DAR-015.

claim: Who gave the order to fire live ammunition, if police did so: NOT ESTABLISHED. Police deny that any live firing by police took place. The High Court says in a passage on the CID's failings that the CID 'may have had serious inhibitions in having to investigate any conspiracy angle that may have led to blaming any police officials for having fired any weapon, or any higher police official ordering such firing into a mob without provocation, at the instance of any person or persons in power' (para 71). The court states this as a possibility about the CID's inhibitions and makes no finding that any such order was given.

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: Quoted because it is the one passage in a primary document that raises the question of an order to fire. It names no officer, office or political figure as having given one. Para 19(h) records the petitioners' submission that only the CBI 'can investigate the role of influential political persons in the incident and the role of the State police in the death of the two boys'; that is the petitioners' submission.

claim: On 23 September 2018 the father of one of the dead men made a complaint that named four people as responsible for the incident: Sumit Kumar, Superintendent of Police, Uttar Dinajpur; Rajen Chettri, Inspector-in-Charge, Islampur; Golam Rabbani, MLA, Islampur constituency; and Kanailal Agarwal, Chairman, Islampur Municipality (judgment para 7). Whether the complaint was received is DISPUTED. The petitioner says the Islampur police station refused to register it and then emailed it to the Chief Secretary (para 7). The State told the court it 'was never sent to or received by either the Islampur P.S. or the CID' (para 27). The court noted that the State had not denied the refusal in its affidavit in opposition and had admitted knowledge of it (para 62(e)), and that the complaint had been annexed to the writ petition filed on 4 October 2018, so it could not be said to have been unknown to the CID (para 62(c)).

sources.publication: Calcutta High Court judgment of 10 May 2023 (Justice Rajasekhar Mantha) in WPA 20733, 20734 and 20938 of 2018, Nilkamal Sarkar, Badal Barman and Subhash Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, copy hosted by Verdictum (not the court's own site)

notes: The complaint names these people as responsible for the incident. The judgment does not say the complaint alleges any of them gave an order, and the court makes no finding against any of them. claim: On 18 November 2019, the first day of the Winter Session of Parliament, students of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) marched from the campus towards Parliament against a hostel fee hike and were stopped by Delhi Police before reaching it, with detentions. NDTV quotes a former students' union president saying the march was stopped about a kilometre from Parliament's north gate.

notes: Level of office: the only institution named in the sources is the Varanasi police. Whether the decision was taken at station level (Chetganj), by the circle officer, the SSP, or on a direction from the district magistrate or from the state police headquarters is unknown. No individual is named, because no primary document read names one. Documents that could settle it are listed in HIST-VNS-015.

claim: Who gave the order for any force used against the group: NOT ESTABLISHED. No source read documents the use of force at Chetganj on 19 December 2019 beyond the FIR's allegation that protesters attacked police and Amnesty's general allegation of excessive force in Varanasi arrests. No order to use force, and no officer who gave one, appears in any source.

claim: A statewide Section 144 CrPC order was announced for Uttar Pradesh for 19 December 2019. The Director General of Police, O. P. Singh, tweeted on 18 December 2019: 'Section 144 (prohibiting unlawful assembly) of CrPC is in force and no permission for any gathering has been given for December 19.' PTI reported that UP police said 'prohibitory orders are in place in the entire state'; Madhyamam reports 'Prohibitory orders under Section 144 of CrPc have been imposed in the whole of Uttar Pradesh.' Scroll.in says the state government imposed Section 144 across the state on 19 December 2019 and names no authority.
notes: What is established: the DGP announced the order and no permission for gatherings was given. What is not: which authority legally issued it and signed it. The sources read do not reproduce the order, its number or its signatory. Scroll's wording ('the state government') and the DGP's tweet are the only attributions. Under the CrPC such orders are ordinarily made by district magistrates or other authorised executive magistrates, but this archive makes no claim about who made this one without the document. The sources are PTI-based and a Kerala newspaper, so independence is limited.

claim: Separate local Section 144 orders were also in force in Varanasi in December 2019. SabrangIndia (4 January 2020) reports orders from 11 December 2019 to 5 February 2020, and earlier ones from 16 October to 9 December 2019. It attributes them to the local administration and police, and quotes Additional District Magistrate Vinod Kumar Singh, who said of the number of days in 2019 'After checking the records, we would only confirm'. The article names no signatory of the orders.
notes: Single source. The ADM is named in the source as a quoted official. No document says he signed or ordered anything, and this archive makes no such claim. Whether these local orders or the statewide one was the basis for the 19 December arrests is not stated by any source. SabrangIndia says police described the arrest charge as violating prohibitory orders.

claim: FIR and charges. Scroll.in (25 December 2019) reports that 56 activists were charged under Indian Penal Code sections 147, 148, 149, 188, 332, 353 and 341, plus Section 7 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1932. The Quint (20 December 2019) lists the same seven IPC sections, and describes them as covering rioting, rioting while armed, unlawful assembly, disobeying an order duly promulgated by a public servant, hurting a public servant, assault or obstructing a public servant, and wrongful restraint.
notes: The FIR text itself was not read, so this is not VERIFIED. Neither outlet gives the FIR number, the police station of registration or the date of registration. Quint says charges were against those arrested; Scroll says 56 of 69. The two outlets agree on sections, which suggests a common basis in the FIR or police briefing, so they may not be wholly independent. These are charges as alleged by police; no court finding of guilt is recorded.

claim: A separate case concerned pamphlets: SabrangIndia (2 January 2020) reports that three of those granted bail were taken into custody on another charge over distribution of pamphlets related to the protest, booked under Sections 153A and 153B, in an FIR filed against an unknown person, and that they would need fresh bail applications.
notes: Single source. The three are not named here. The outcome of that second bail application is not in any source read.

SabrangIndia: all 56 released, naming Judge Sarvesh Kumar Pandey. PTI via Deccan Herald: bail to a couple (the parents of a 14-month-old child) on Wednesday 1 January 2020 and, per its text, 56 others, while its headline says 56 in all.

Pandey' and Sabrang as 'Sarvesh Kumar Pandey', which may be the same person, and no order was read. Cases had been listed for 1 January 2020 because of the holiday season (Sabrang). claim: Records that could be requested to establish who gave the order. (3) Office of the Varanasi district magistrate: any Section 144 order in force that day, with signatory and date, and any magisterial instruction on the Beniabagh march. Ask the same question at each rung (station, circle, SSP, DM, Home Department) so that any 'not us' reply is itself evidence.

Some aspirants quoted by PTI and Newslaundry say teachers took over the protest, and PTI adds that police in civil dress attacked protesters, per an unnamed aspirant. These are the quoted people's claims.

claim: On 10 November 2025 protesters demanding that Panjab University announce its Senate election schedule broke through police barricades and forced Gate No. 1 of the Chandigarh campus. Police used a lathicharge. PTI, in The Hindu, calls it a 'mild lathicharge to restore order'; The Indian Express says 'A lathicharge was carried out to bring the situation under control.'

sources.publication: The Hindu (PTI), 10 November 2025, updated 4:39 pm IST
The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Deepankar Sharda and Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025
The Times of India (TNN), Akashdeep Virk, 10 November 2025, 13:10 IST

notes: Occurrence corroborated by four outlets. No primary document (police report, university statement, court order) was read. The force is described as 'mild' by PTI, the Tribune and the police-attributed accounts; no source read gives an independent measure of it. Tribune pages were read through a summarising fetch tool and not verbatim; quotations in this file come only from the Hindu, Indian Express, Hindustan Times and Times of India pages, which were read in full.

claim: The protest followed the Union government's 28 October 2025 notification restructuring Panjab University's Senate and Syndicate. The Indian Express reports the Ministry of Education withdrew it on 7 November 2025; students continued the agitation demanding that the Senate election schedule be announced.

sources.publication: The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025

notes: Context record. LiveLaw's report of the High Court order says the amendments were withdrawn on 4 November and notifications reserving the right to constitute the Senate were rescinded on 7 November 2025; the sources differ on the 4 November step, not on 7 November. Hindustan Times adds that the university sent a poll schedule to the Vice-President's office on 9 November 2025.

claim: Size of the police deployment on 10 November 2025 is given differently: about 2,500 Union Territory police personnel at the gates and inside campus from 5:30 am plus 150 to 200 Punjab Police personnel called in (Tribune); over 2,700 personnel (Tribune); over 2,000 personnel (Hindustan Herald).

sources.publication: The Tribune, Sheetal, Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Nitin Jain and Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025

notes: Versions: (a) 2,500 UT police plus 150-200 Punjab Police, Tribune 'Police struggle to contain violent protest'; (b) over 2,700, Tribune 'Campus stormed'; (c) over 2,000, Herald. None attributes the figure to a named officer. Who requested the Punjab Police contingent is not stated in any source read. Water cannons were reported on standby (Tribune). Haryana Police assistance appeared only in a search snippet of a Congress statement and was not fetched; do not use.

claim: Hindustan Times reports that the Union Territory administration had imposed 'Section 223 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) across Chandigarh, prohibiting gatherings of five or more persons', and that police cited this order to the crowd at Gate No. 1.
notes: Single source. The issuing office and officer are not named, and no order text was found. The section label needs checking: HT also lists Section 223 of the BNS (disobedience to a public servant's order) in the FIR. The BNSS provision for prohibitory orders is believed to be Section 163, but this was not verified against the statute text. A January 2026 Tribune report of a later PIL refers to a District Magistrate order under Section 163 BNSS limiting rallies to the Sector 25 Rally Ground; that order's date and relation to 10 November are not stated. Request the actual order (see notes file).

claim: Detentions on 10 November 2025. The Indian Express reports 'Around 80 protesters were detained under preventive measures but were released later in the evening' and that police stopped 400 to 500 protesters from entering the city. The Tribune reports students who tried to force entry at Gates 1 and 2 were taken to the IRB Complex, Sarangpur, and released later; SSP Chandigarh is quoted saying those held 'were not detained' but managed in a controlled manner, and that police ensured 'no tear gas, water cannons or excessive force was used'.

sources.publication: The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Sheetal, Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Deepankar Sharda and Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025

notes: The 80 figure appears in one source (Indian Express, in its own voice, not attributed to a named police officer). Other Tribune pieces say 'several' students were detained or taken away and give no number. The SSP's reported denial that anyone was detained conflicts with the Indian Express wording 'detained under preventive measures'. No legal provision for the detentions is named in any source; no detention memo or list was found. The SSP quotes come from a summarising fetch of the Tribune page and should be checked verbatim.

claim: Injuries on 10 November 2025. Hindustan Times, citing the FIR, and the Tribune report four police personnel injured at Gate No. 1: a DSP, an inspector, a senior constable and a sub-inspector, taken to GMSH Sector 16 and discharged after first aid. The Indian Express says the IG 'confirmed that no injuries were reported'. The Tribune quotes the SSP as saying 'No one was injured or harmed', in an article that also reports police injuries. No source read reports an injury to a protester.

sources.publication: The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Sheetal, Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Tribune News Service, updated 17 November 2025

notes: The sources do not say whether the IG's and SSP's statements referred only to protesters. The reading that they meant protesters is an inference and is not stated by any source. No hospital record, MLC or police report was read. Absence of reported protester injuries in the press is not evidence that none occurred.

claim: Sources describe the crowd on 10 November 2025 as a mix: students including leaders of the Panjab University Bachao Morcha, farmer union members (including Bharatiya Kisan Union and Samyukt Kisan Morcha-linked groups), Nihangs and Sikh organisation activists, and political figures. The Indian Express says the demonstration 'saw the participation of student leaders as well as several farmer union members'. The Tribune says as many as 50 organisations and student groups supported the call.

sources.publication: The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025
The Tribune, Deepankar Sharda and Tribune News Service, updated 11 November 2025

notes: Composition is qualitative only. No source gives a count of students against non-students. Named politicians and individuals are omitted here.

claim: The Indian Express reports that police 'failed to stop the large group from entering the campus, many of whom were reportedly not students', and quotes the IG as saying 'many outsiders who had joined the protest began moving back towards Mohali' by evening. Hindustan Times reports the FIR alleges both PU students and outsiders were involved at Gate No. 1.

sources.publication: The Indian Express, Jagpreet Singh Sandhu, 11 November 2025

notes: 'Reportedly' is the Indian Express's own hedge; it names no source. The FIR account (as reported by HT) alleges students inside the campus broke the chain and lock with stones while outsiders outside removed barricades, which is an allegation by police, not a finding. Student leaders told the Tribune live blog the police and administration were 'controlling tents, sound systems, and logistics without Vice Chancellor approval' (summarised, unverified). The 'not students' statement is therefore attributed and unquantified.

claim: Who gave the order for the lathicharge and for the preventive detentions on 10 November 2025: no page read names the officer or office that ordered either. The sources name the IG and the SSP Chandigarh as present at the gate, and say they were forced to leave when the crowd broke the gate; their presence is not an order.
notes: Not established. No order, deployment plan or station diary was found. The Tribune live blog says the IG and SSP arrived at 11:46 am and left when the gate was forced; a 'mild lathicharge' followed. The Tribune also carries 'sources claimed the cops were restrained from taking a tough action' (summarised). File RTIs as listed in the notes file.

claim: Who requested or ordered the 10 November 2025 police deployment, and whether Panjab University's administration asked for police: no page read says. Hindustan Herald says the administration's response included 'summon[ing] police' without naming who or when; this is a summary-tool paraphrase of an unattributed sentence and is not relied on.
notes: Not established. What is reported: the university announced holidays on 10 and 11 November and restricted entry to ID holders (record 12); the Vice-Chancellor appealed for restraint (Tribune); the university filed a police complaint on 15 November 2025 (record 11). None of these is a request for police deployment on 10 November.

claim: Hindustan Times reports that 'On Saturday', 15 November 2025, the university filed a police complaint alleging trespassing and destruction of property during the 10 November protest.
notes: Single source, one sentence. The complaint was not read; who signed it is not stated. HT's article is dated 17 November 2025, so 'Saturday' is 15 November.

claim: Before the protest the university announced holidays on 10 and 11 November 2025 and allowed only people with university ID cards to enter campus; police barricaded entry points and set up checkpoints, including at the Chandigarh-Mohali border.
notes: The university announced the closure and ID-only entry according to Careers360 (PTI-based) and the Herald. Who set the ID-only rule, the university or police, is not stated; Hindustan Times attributes the gate restrictions to police.

claim: Chandigarh Police registered an FIR against unidentified students and outsiders for the 10 November 2025 events at Gate No. 1. Hindustan Times reports it was lodged on the statement of a sub-inspector, under BNS sections 221, 223, 191(2), 190, 115(2), 121(1) and 132, after verification against a daily diary report (DDR) of 10 November, and that footage from government photographers and videographers would be used to identify the accused. The Tribune reports the Sector 11 police registered the case.

sources.publication: The Tribune, Tribune News Service, updated 17 November 2025

notes: FIR number and date of registration not stated in either report and the FIR was not read. HT places the complainant at the Sector 31 police station; the Tribune says Sector 11 police registered the case, which may be the registering station against the complainant's posting. Both outlets say the accused are unidentified. HT says the sub-inspector 'did not know the identities of the accused'. The Tribune on 18 November 2025 speaks of a 'fresh FIR' for the 10 November bandh; whether this is the same FIR was not established. Section numbers are as reported and not checked against the BNS text.

claim: Punjab and Haryana High Court, Harpreet Singh Dua and another v. Panjab University and others (a 2024 petition seeking Senate elections): a bench of Chief Justice Sheel Nagu and Justice Sanjiv Berry, per LiveLaw, told students academic work 'cannot be compromised or sacrificed at the altar of electoral or political aspirations', expressed hope Senate elections would be held as soon as possible, and disposed of the plea. Hindustan Times reports the High Court 'on Friday' asked protesting students to return to classes.
notes: The order was not read. LiveLaw's article is dated 18 November 2025; HT of 17 November 2025 says Friday, which is 14 November 2025, so the hearing date is inferred and unconfirmed. Per LiveLaw's summary the order does not mention 10 November, police action, outsiders or any FIR. It concerns the delay in Senate elections, not police conduct.

notes: Absence of evidence. Searches covered Tribune, LiveLaw and general web; eCourts, the High Court site and Indian Kanoon were not searched directly. Check them for habeas, writ or quashing petitions against the FIR.

claim: The 27-day Panjab University Bachao Morcha dharna ended on the night of 28 November 2025 after the Vice-Chancellor handed over a written resolution. The Tribune reports that students seeking FIR relief submit individual written requests and the university forwards them 'to the competent authority for appropriate action'. Withdrawal of the FIRs was one of the Morcha's demands (Hindustan Times).

sources.publication: The Tribune, Nitin Jain and Tribune News Service, updated 29 November 2025

notes: The resolution document was not read. Neither source says any FIR was withdrawn. The Tribune is dated 29 November 2025 and says the dharna was called off 'the night before'.
